## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)
*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*
The *Kharaputtajātaka* (Ja 386) is a narrative text belonging to the Pali *Jātaka* collection [SuttaCentral]. According to the canonical frame narrative preserved in its commentary, the Buddha delivered this teaching while residing at Jetavana to address a monk tempted to leave the monastic order by his former wife [SuttaCentral; Fausböll 1883]. The Master noted that the woman had caused him peril in a previous existence, wherein he had been rescued from death by the wise [SuttaCentral].
In the story of the past, Senaka, king of Benares, saves a Nāga king who was on the verge of being slain by boys while seeking food on earth [de Visser 1913]. Later, following a false accusation made by a Nāga maiden appointed to watch over the king, the quick-tempered Nāga ruler sends four youths to assassinate Senaka with their venomous breath [de Visser 1913]. The narrative also features animal dialogue involving a horse and a goat [Doniger 2010; Fausböll 1883]. When King Senaka foolishly intends to reveal a secret charm to his wife even though doing so would forfeit his own life, the Bodhisatta intervenes in the guise of Sakka transformed into a goat, convincing him to protect his life rather than satisfy his wife's demand [Anandajoti 2010]. In the *samodhāna*, the Buddha reveals that the infatuated king was the tempted monk, the queen was his former wife, the horse was Sāriputta, and Sakka was the Bodhisatta himself [Fausböll 1883].

DharmaNexus records no cross-language parallels with a score of 10 or greater [DharmaNexus]. SuttaCentral records four translations across four modern languages [SuttaCentral].
